title: Discovering Symmetry Groups with Flow Matching
one_liner: LieFlow discovers what symmetries (rotations, reflections, repetitions) exist in data by learning which transformations leave the data unchanged.
lead: Physical systems and real-world data often have hidden symmetries—patterns that stay the same under certain transformations like rotation or reflection. Finding these symmetries automatically is hard, yet knowing them can make machine learning models faster and more accurate. LieFlow solves this by treating symmetry discovery as a learning problem: instead of searching for the symmetry generators, it learns a probability model (assigning confidence scores to each candidate symmetry), and the candidate symmetries with the highest scores reveal which ones actually exist in the data.

paras: A symmetry is a transformation that leaves something unchanged. A square looks the same after a 90-degree rotation, or flipped across a diagonal. Real data—point clouds from 3D scanners, molecular structures, images—often has symmetries baked in. A naive approach searches through a list of candidate symmetries and checks which ones work. But the list is huge, and discrete symmetries (like reflection) are especially hard to spot—you can easily miss them.

The bottleneck: symmetry search requires testing millions of possible transformations, and testing is expensive. Moreover, if your hypothesis space is incomplete or biased toward certain symmetry types, you will miss the real ones.

callout.html: LieFlow learns to score candidate symmetries (assigning high scores to real ones, low scores to false ones); the high-scoring candidates are the actual symmetries.

object.h2: What changes: scoring function for symmetry candidates
paras: The paper does not search for individual symmetries one by one. Instead, it learns a single object: a probability distribution defined over the entire space of symmetries (a Lie group or other group structure). The support of that distribution—the region where probability is high—automatically reveals which symmetries exist in the data. This is a shift from generate-and-test to learn-and-read-off.

hidden.name: per-transformation probability
paras: The paper's core hidden quantity is the probability assigned to each possible transformation. For a rotation by angle theta, or a reflection across plane X, what is the model's confidence that this transformation is a real symmetry of the data? In flow matching, this is learned implicitly by training a velocity field (a continuous map) that guides samples through group space toward high-density regions.

The paper estimates this via the learned flow model: sample elements from the group, evaluate them under the trained model, and rank by score. Transformations that score highest (the modes) are the actual symmetries.

heat.caption: Darker means higher probability the model assigns. True symmetries are marked; they get high scores.

reads.html: The model learns: identity (always works), 90-degree rotations (this cube has 4-fold symmetry), and horizontal/diagonal flips (if the object is symmetric). Random transformations get low scores.

The learned flow model on the Lie group or discrete group induces a probability density. The paper uses the model to rank candidate transformations; elements mapping to high probability are the symmetries.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: flow matching learns where symmetries concentrate
paras: Flow matching is a technique that trains a model to smoothly move points from a simple starting state (random) toward target states where data is invariant. Here, the target is implicitly defined: transformations that leave data unchanged (symmetries) should score high, and random transformations should score low.

The method defines a velocity field on group space (a continuous map that points in the direction of higher scores). During training, the model learns to nudge samples toward score peaks where data is invariant under those transformations. Unlike testing each symmetry one by one, this is a single optimization where the model learns one velocity function that steers all samples toward the true symmetry peaks at once. Once trained, you can sample or optimize in this learned direction, and high-scoring clusters appear automatically. Because flow matching handles both continuous symmetries (rotations) and discrete symmetries (reflections) with the same machinery, it avoids building separate pipelines for each type.

stages.s: Data (point cloud) + large hypothesis group G
Define invariance: test each group element for data invariance
Train flow model on group space to assign high probability to invariant elements
Sample or optimize in learned distribution to find modes

math.words: Minimize the difference between a learned velocity field and a target velocity that transitions from noise to invariant transformations.
math.equation: L = E[ ||v(g_t, t) - u_t(g)||^2 ] where g_t is a path in group space parameterized by time t, v is the learned velocity, u_t is the target velocity.
symbols: transformation at time t (element of group space)
learned velocity field predicting direction in group space
target velocity field derived from data invariance
average over all training examples and time steps

worked.title: Tiny numeric example
lines: Consider a rotation group: angles from 0 to 360 degrees.
Sample paths: start at random angles (50°, 180°, 290°), end at true symmetry (90°).
Target velocity u_t: angle should drift smoothly from start toward 90°.
Learned velocity v: model predicts how fast angle should change at each step.
Loss at step 1: v predicts +5°/step, target is +8°/step, squared error 9.
Loss at step 2: v predicts +7°/step, target is +6°/step, squared error 1.
Average: training reduces error by learning v to match u_t, guiding samples to symmetry peaks.

math.note: The flow model acts as a compass in group space, pointing samples toward regions where transformations leave data unchanged.

items.html: If the group G does not contain the true symmetries, the method cannot find them, because no score can favor what is not in the search space. Choosing too small a group (e.g., only rotations when the data also has reflections) means the learned model scores reflections as low even though they are real.

Real data is never perfectly symmetric. If noise is high relative to the true invariances, the learned distribution may spread across many plausible transformations rather than concentrating at true peaks.
If multiple distinct symmetries explain the data equally well, the learned distribution may have multiple high-probability modes. You must decide how many to keep.

Choose a hypothesis group that is plausible for the domain. Collect enough clean data. Use the learned distribution's confidence (entropy or peak sharpness) to judge whether symmetries are genuinely there or are artifacts.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small experiment on synthetic data: generate a point cloud with a known symmetry (e.g., a square rotated by 90 degrees), train LieFlow to learn the distribution over rotations and reflections, and check that the model assigns high probability to the true symmetry (90-degree rotation) and low probability to random transformations. Then test on data where discrete symmetries exist (a vertically flipped rectangle) and confirm the model finds the reflection. Finally, compare discovery accuracy (fraction of true symmetries correctly ranked in the top k) and wall-clock time versus a naive baseline that tests all hypotheses one by one.
demo.metric_eq: accuracy = (true symmetries correctly in top-k) / (total true symmetries); speedup = baseline_time / lieflow_time
demo.closing: The demo is successful if LieFlow finds both continuous and discrete symmetries faster than exhaustive search (because one model replaces many individual tests) and with fewer false positives (because the learned score concentrates at true symmetries, not noise).
